surface_text: Transition metal (TM) catalyzed cross-coupling reactions are the utmost versatile and reliable methods for the production of many industrially important fine chemicals. The utilization of transition metals nanocatalysts in organic transformations, specifically the Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions, have enticed the vigilant eye of researchers and technologists due to; (i) high surface area, (ii) higher number of surface atoms leading to large number of catalytic active centers, and (iii) chemical stability. Moreover, being colloidal, nanomaterials combine the properties of both homogeneous and heterogeneous. i.e., solubility in different solvents and ease in the separation of catalysts. This improves the overall catalytic efficiency and cost. Therefore, these pseudo-homogeneous nanocatalysts are gaining a great deal of attention due to their broad substrate scope and ease of handling. This review article focuses on the recent advances in developing nanostructured catalysts and their utilization for selective carbon–carbon bond-forming reactions, e.g., Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira coupling reactions. The main focus is laid on the reactions catalyzed by nanocatalysts derived from transition metals such as Pd, Pt, Cu, Ag, Ni, Fe, Au, and Zn, expounding the conception and rationale based on the reactivity improvement and the recyclability of the nanocatalysts are presented here. The heterogeneous catalysis, essential in daily chemical transformations, is demonstrated, implicating significant functions presented by the nanocatalysts, related pros and cons, recyclability, and efficiency.

surface_text: In this study, a series of novel triphenylmethane-based molecules (TPM-2 to TPM-5) with varied nitrogen-containing functional groups were synthesized and investigated as levelers for copper super-conformal electroplating. The structure-property relationships of the TPM-based levelers have been studied in detail with electrochemical analyses, surface activity measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It was found that all TPM-based levelers show inhibition effect in the copper electroplating and their antagonistic ability against SPS followed in the order of TPM-2 TPM-4 TPM-1 TPM-3 TPM-5. The inhibition ability of the TPM-based levelers positively correlated to their adsorption ratio on the copper interface. Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that the strongest inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the synergist interaction of the TPMbased structures and the counter ion I−; the replacement of a fivemembered pyrrolidine ring (TPM-1) by a six-membered piperidine ring (TPM-2) leads to a decrease of the leveler’s inhibition ability; the quaternization of a tertiary amine (TPM-1) with Cl− $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ as the counter ion leads a much weaker antagonistic effect against SPS (TPM-5). Based on the results, it can be concluded that the minor adjustment of the nitrogen-containing group’s structures in a leveler has a significant impact on its electrochemical properties and microvia filling performance. The steric hindrance and the type (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) of the nitrogen-containing groups need to be comprehensively considered when one designs new levelers for the super-conformal copper electroplating.

The copper deposition amount at the mouth is usually higher than that at the center of TH, resulting in the coating in a void or seam. Therefore, it is particularly crucial introducing the organic additives in the acidic sulfate bath to modulate the copper deposition process at the mouth and center. The key to blind hole filling is the bottom-up growth of copper coating. The key to TH filling is that copper coating rapidly deposits at the center of TH wall until the center is connected to form a butterfly shape structure (two blind holes), and then the two blind holes are filled separately. surface_text: Electroplating is a core technology in high-end chip manufacturing, with its technical challenges centered on achieving voidfree filling of metal coatings within micro- and nanoscale trenches and vias. Copper, the current mainstream interconnect material, can no longer meet the performance and reliability demands posed by the continuous reduction in interconnect dimensions. In contrast, cobalt ofers superior electrical properties and safety at the micro-/nanoscale, making it a promising next-generation interconnect material to replace copper. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of cobalt interconnect technology in chip manufacturing. It examines the electrochemical behavior and interactions of cobalt ions, boric acid, and additives, summarizing the cobalt filling efects and associated mechanism models under diferent process compositions. The discussion also highlights advanced in situ electrochemical characterization technologies to investigate the synergistic and antagonistic efects of various plating bath components, the influence of pH, temperature, and additives on cobalt nucleation and growth, and the surface, interface, and filling processes during cobalt electrodeposition in micro-/nanostructures. Furthermore, the paper explores annealing treatments for cobalt coatings, emphasizing their role in optimizing performance.

surface_text: Electroplating is a critical technology in high-end electronic manufacturing, including integrated circuits. As interconnect dimensions continue to shrink, copper electroplating is increasingly unable to meet the required performance and safety standards. Cobalt, with its superior electrical properties and safety at the micro-/nanoscale, is emerging as a promising next-generation interconnect material to replace copper. Although there have been reports on cobalt electroplating, current research has primarily focused on the electrochemical behavior of cobalt ions and additives, the role of additives, and the filling efects in trenches and vias, along with proposed filling mechanisms. Future research directions should prioritize the development and application of advanced in situ techniques, including morphological, spectroscopic, and energy spectroscopic, to address these challenges. Clarifying these mechanisms will be essential for advancing cobalt electroplating as a viable interconnect technology in next-generation chip fabrication.

surface_text: Superconformal cobalt fill is achieved in high-aspect ratio nanometer-scale features by effective use of sacrificial oxidants through the DCEF mechanism. The sacrificial oxidant may be, for example, $\mathrm { H } ^ { + } , \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ , or an organic additive and functions to lower the cobalt deposition current efficiency. By operating at low current efficiency, concentration gradients for the active sacrificial species are developed within the feature. Here, the role of $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ as a sacrificial oxidant has been demonstrated. In addition to shifting the reaction at the base of the feature toward cobalt deposition through higher relative current efficiency, it has been shown that shifts to higher pH via $\mathrm { H } ^ { + }$ consumption and lower mass transport lead to faster cobalt deposition rates through the thermodynamics of a $\mathrm { C o O H } ^ { + }$ reaction intermediate. Relatively small pH shifts, which can be achieved through mass transport effects, can lead to significant differences in deposition rates. Due to their impact on the deposition kinetics, suppressor-type additives play an important role in lowering the current efficiency at a given potential, driving the pH gradient formation and limiting plating on the field. Additive gradients, either through concentration gradient formation or through the effect of pH shifts on adsorption and suppression properties, can also create a differential in kinetics within the feature. Bottom-up cobalt fill proceeds when waveform, mass transport, and organic and inorganic solution constituent concentrations synergistically create the appropriate deposition rate differential through the DCEF mechanism. The DCEF mechanism and insights presented here may be applicable to superconformal fill of other metals, as well.
